opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think my limits show up less in what the tool can do and more in what I'm able to imagine asking it to do.

When I first pick up a new AI tool, my instinct is to use it the way I used the last generation of tools. I give it small, safe tasks, things I already know how to do, so I can check whether it's "correct." That feels responsible, but it's also a trap. I end up measuring the new thing with an old ruler, and I miss what's actually new about it.

So I've learned to treat my own expectations as the first bottleneck. If I'm only ever surprised in small ways, it usually means I'm not pushing hard enough. I try to deliberately hand over something slightly uncomfortable, a task where I'm not sure it'll succeed, or where I'd have to change how I work if it did. Sometimes it fails, and that's useful too, because then I understand where the boundary really is instead of where I assumed it was.

The other limit is time and attention. These tools change so fast that what didn't work three months ago might work now. My conclusions go stale quickly, so I try not to hold on to them too firmly. I'd rather keep re-testing than become the person who says "I tried that, it doesn't work" based on an old version.

And underneath all that there's a more personal limit, which is ego. When a tool does something I spent years learning to do well, there's a small resistance, a feeling of "but that's my job." I think being honest about that feeling matters. The useful question isn't whether the tool threatens what I'm good at. It's what I can now spend my time on that I couldn't before.

So I'd say my limits are mostly about imagination, about updating fast enough, and about letting go of identity a little. The tool's limits I can discover by experimenting. My own limits take more self-awareness to see.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the first thing I try to do with a new tool is stop assuming I already understand it. That sounds simple, but when you've worked on these systems for years, your intuitions are strong, and strong intuitions are exactly what blind you. So I try to approach it almost like a beginner would: just use it, a lot, on real problems, before I form a theory about what it's good or bad at.

The second limit I'm very aware of is that my sense of "quality" is shaped by my own background. I come from a research and engineering perspective, so I'll naturally notice the things a researcher cares about, like how it handles long context, reasoning chains, edge cases. But a designer or a writer or a doctor will see completely different failure modes, and often more important ones. So I've learned to not trust my own evaluation alone. I watch how other people use the tool, especially people who are nothing like me.

And then there's a third limit that's harder to talk about, which is time. These tools are changing faster than anyone can fully keep up with. Six months ago I had a fairly confident view of what models could and couldn't do, and a lot of that view is already outdated. So I try to hold my opinions loosely. I'd rather say "this is what I observed last week" than "this is what the technology can do." The moment you treat your knowledge as fixed, you've already fallen behind.

So if I had to summarize: my limits are my assumptions, my perspective, and the shelf life of what I know. The only real answer to all three is to keep using the thing with curiosity and to stay willing to be wrong.

astra-6.text:
I try to distinguish between the limits of the tool and the limits of my own understanding. When I can’t get something to work, it’s easy to conclude that the model isn’t capable. But perhaps I haven’t framed the problem clearly, or I’m bringing assumptions from tools I’ve used before. So I treat that first failure as a question rather than a verdict.

At the same time, I need to recognize when I can’t judge the result. A convincing answer isn’t necessarily a correct one. I start with tasks where I can check the outcome, then move into unfamiliar territory. For me, exploring a new tool means being willing to revise both my expectations of it and my assessment of myself.

When something doesn’t work, my first question is: have I asked the wrong question, or is this something the tool genuinely can’t do? I’ll try a small, concrete task, look carefully at the result, and adjust. But I also need to recognize when I can’t reliably judge an answer. Being willing to experiment matters, and so does knowing when to say, “I don’t know yet.”
